titulo: Inversion, Cleft and Fronting for Emphasis
descripcion: At C2 the three emphasis devices — inversion, cleft, fronting — are deployed across a whole argumentative passage, alternating deliberately so no single device dominates the register. The C1 skill was building each correctly; the C2 skill is knowing when restraint matters more than density.

filas: shifts focus without a heavy structure
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: A passage that opens AND closes with heavy inversion reads as performative. Reserve the heaviest device for one location only.

ejemplos.texto: What the data ultimately reveals is not a trend but a reversal.
That much, the committee could agree on; the rest remained contested.
Only in hindsight did the full cost become apparent.

notas: Across a full passage, using all three devices in sequence without variation reads as mechanical, even when each is individually correct.
The strongest placement for a negative inversion is the close of a paragraph, where it lands with full weight.
A cleft at the opening sets the reader's expectation for the whole argument that follows — misuse there derails more than a single sentence.

es.en: Spanish builds the same kind of rhetorical architecture by varying word order freely across a paragraph, without a fixed structure at each point of emphasis. Spanish speakers at C2 therefore tend to repeat the same type of cleft out of habit instead of alternating the three devices as refined English expects.
es.es: El español construye una arquitectura retórica similar variando libremente el orden de las palabras a lo largo de un párrafo, sin una estructura fija para cada punto de énfasis. Por eso, los hispanohablantes de C2 tienden a repetir por hábito el mismo tipo de cleft, en lugar de alternar los tres recursos como espera un inglés más refinado.

de.en: Because German is verb-second, fronting is the default German way to emphasise (Das akzeptiere ich nicht), and clefts are used less than in English. German speakers therefore lean on fronting (This I cannot accept), which is strongly marked in English, and need to consciously bring in clefts and inversion to vary the passage.
de.de: Weil Deutsch Verbzweitstellung hat, ist Voranstellung die normale deutsche Betonungsstrategie («Das akzeptiere ich nicht»), während clefts seltener sind. Deutschsprachige neigen deshalb zu Fronting («This I cannot accept»), das im Englischen stark markiert ist, und müssen clefts und inversion bewusst einsetzen, um stilistisch zu variieren.

it.en: Italian highlights through free order, clefts and left-dislocation with a resumptive pronoun (Il rapporto, l'ho letto). Italian speakers therefore tend to over-use clefts and to transfer dislocation (The report, I read it), which is non-standard in written English.
it.it: L'italiano mette in rilievo tramite ordine libero, cleft e dislocazione a sinistra con pronome ripreso («Il rapporto, l'ho letto»). Gli italofoni tendono quindi a usare troppo i cleft e a trasferire la dislocazione («The report, I read it»), non standard nell'inglese scritto.

fr.en: Spoken and written French emphasises mainly through clefts (c'est… qui/que) and dislocation (Ce rapport, je l'ai lu). French speakers therefore over-use it-clefts and may transfer dislocation, and need to bring inversion and fronting into the mix deliberately.
fr.fr: Le français parlé et écrit met surtout l'accent grâce aux clivées («c'est… qui/que») et à la dislocation («Ce rapport, je l'ai lu»). Les francophones abusent donc des it-clefts, peuvent transférer la dislocation, et doivent introduire consciemment inversion et fronting pour varier.

pt.en: Brazilian Portuguese often fronts a topic without a resumptive pronoun (Isso eu não aceito), which maps neatly onto English fronting (This I cannot accept). Clefts with é que are also frequent, so Portuguese speakers have both tools; what needs practice is inversion and the deliberate alternation of all three.
pt.pt: O português brasileiro frequentemente antepõe um tópico sem pronome resumptivo («Isso eu não aceito»), o que se encaixa bem no fronting inglês («This I cannot accept»). Clefts com «é que» também são frequentes, então falantes de português já têm dois recursos; o que precisa ser praticado é inversion e a alternância deliberada dos três.

errores: Opening and closing a passage with the same heavy device, which reads as performative rather than controlled.
Repeating the same type of cleft throughout instead of alternating with fronting and inversion.
Using negative inversion mid-paragraph where it doesn't carry the argument's final weight.

autochequeo: Are the three devices alternated across the passage, not repeated identically?
Is the heaviest device (negative inversion) reserved for a single, weighted location?
Does the opening cleft accurately set up the argument that follows?
Would a native reader sense control across the whole passage, not just in isolated sentences?
Is there at least one paragraph without any of these devices, for contrast?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on how inversion, cleft and fronting are distributed across the whole passage. Flag repetition of the same device and check whether the heaviest one is reserved for a single weighted point. Do not rewrite the text.

es: Keeping the resumptive clitic of Spanish topicalisation («*este libro lo he leído*»): *This book I have read it* instead of *This book I have read*.
de: *gerade* rendered as *straight*: *Straight that is the point* instead of *That is precisely the point*.
it: Keeping the resumptive clitic of Italian topicalisation («*questo libro l'ho letto*»): *This book I have read it* instead of *This book I have read*.
fr: Keeping the resumptive pronoun of French dislocation («*ce livre, je l'ai lu*»): *This book, I have read it* instead of *This book I have read*.
pt: Keeping the resumptive clitic of Portuguese topicalisation («*este livro, li-o*»): *This book, I read it* instead of *This book I read*.
